A equipe não encontrou água acumulada junto às fileiras um a oito, nem na faixa entre as fileiras dez e doze. A folha de serviço ficou com Rui, junto do desenho simples do setor norte. The sky was clear over the ridge, but low cloud covered the western spur, and there was a cold wind coming up the drainage. I wrote the date as the eighteenth of June and the crew as Mara Chen and Elliot Price, with Tomas Reed joining us after lunch. The barometer read nine hundred and twelve hectopascals, and the phone showed an elevation of one thousand four hundred and eighty metres. We did not treat the phone elevation as a survey value because the canopy and the steep wall made the signal unreliable.

The main exposure is a pale grey limestone ledge about thirty metres long, with a darker brown band crossing it from southwest to northeast. The return involved instruments, science kits, sports gear, and two carts of library tablets that had been borrowed for the sixth grade project week. Ms. Ellis was coordinating the return with Mr. Chen from facilities and Nina Patel, the student council treasurer. The equipment had come from three storage rooms and several classrooms, so the staff wanted one shared record before anything was moved back to its usual shelf. The gym doors stayed open, but the west side entrance remained locked during delivery.

The first cart arrived at eight twenty with twenty-four tablets in padded sleeves and a small box of charging blocks. The inventory sheet listed twenty-six sleeves, but two had been set aside in the library for a repair check. The office had emailed that detail on Wednesday, although the printed sheet did not include it. Ms. Ellis said, “Please keep the two repair sleeves separate from the returning equipment and write their location on the blue tag.” Mr. Chen placed the blue tag beside the box rather than attaching it to either sleeve because the sleeves were still in the library. He asked Nina to confirm the charger count before the cart went through the gym doors.

Nina counted twenty-four charging blocks and found one block with a cracked corner. The class teacher had written that the tablets were all present but had not counted the blocks. Ms. Ellis compared the cart list with the email and entered twenty-four blocks as present and one as pending review. The cart remained beside the eastern wall while Nina looked for the aide. The return could continue if the pending item stayed clearly separate and was not mixed into the closed box.

The return checklist had three numbered entries:
1. Count each item against the room sheet and record any difference.
2. Attach a location tag to equipment that is being held for review.
3. Move only the counted equipment to its assigned storage area.

The list applied to all departments and not only to the tablet cart. Mr. Chen read each entry aloud because the gym was noisy with chairs being stacked nearby. Ms. Ellis asked that the storage room number be written on each tag, and Nina agreed to use the labels from the supply cabinet. The checklist did not give permission to discard or repair anything, and the staff had no plan to do either.

At nine ten, the band teacher brought two instrument cases, a stand, and a folder of mouthpiece covers. The sticker gave a location but no staff name, so Mr. Chen left it visible for a later check.

The science teacher arrived with three sealed kit boxes and one open tray of glass slides. The boxes matched the list, but the tray had a handwritten note that said, “Inspect before storage.” The teacher explained that the class had used the tray for a demonstration and had returned every slide to its slot. Ms. Ellis said the tray could stay in the gym until the lab aide confirmed the note because the condition on the return sheet required any item marked “Inspect before storage” to remain outside the science room. The teacher took the three sealed boxes to the assigned cart and left the tray on a padded table with the note facing upward.

The tablets and charging blocks that had been counted were placed on the technology cart. The cracked block was in a small envelope marked “Pending review.” The two repair sleeves remained in the library, and the blue tag named the library as their location. The band cases were placed on the music cart while the stand and mouthpiece folder stayed on the table. The sealed science kits were on the lab cart, and the slide tray remained on the padded table. No one moved an item from one area to another without telling Ms. Ellis and writing the reason on the shared sheet.

The school secretary called at eleven to ask if everything had been returned because a delivery van was scheduled to collect empty storage bins after lunch. Nina said the return was still in progress and gave the secretary the count from the sheet. She did not report the pending items as missing and did not say that the return was complete. The Saturday shift at the Harbor Street charity kitchen began before sunrise, while rain tapped against the loading-bay door and the street outside was still quiet. Mara, the shift coordinator, unlocked the pantry at 5:45 and checked the whiteboard before anyone started cooking. The plan was to serve lunch to about 140 people, but the number was only an estimate because the nearby shelter had reported several new arrivals overnight. Mara said, “Let’s prepare enough for the estimate, and keep the extra rice dry until we know how many guests are coming.” That decision mattered later, when the shelter called with an updated count.

Six volunteers arrived between six and six-thirty. Two had worked the kitchen before; the others were first-time helpers from a local college. Mara paired each new volunteer with someone who knew the room, then showed everyone where the hand-washing sink, gloves, fire blanket, and first-aid kit were kept. The kitchen’s printed temperature chart was clipped beside the refrigerator, and Leon checked the cooler before moving in the donated vegetables. It read 38 degrees Fahrenheit, within the kitchen’s safe range. A box of tomatoes had split during delivery, so the volunteers set aside the damaged fruit for immediate use rather than placing it in storage. The remaining produce was counted and recorded on the donation sheet.

The menu included lentil stew, rice, roasted carrots, bread, and apples. A donor had brought carrots from a neighborhood garden, along with a note saying they had been harvested the previous afternoon. Priya rinsed and peeled them while Ben cut them into even pieces. Mara asked the team to keep the vegetable scraps in the marked compost bin, not the regular trash. The lentils had already been sorted the night before, but the cooking group still rinsed them in batches and checked for small stones. When the large stockpot reached a steady simmer, Leon lowered the heat so the bottom would not scorch. He tasted a spoonful and said, “It needs a little more salt, but let’s wait until the broth has reduced.” Nobody added seasoning until the next tasting.

1. At 7:10, Mara divided the remaining preparation work. The first table washed and portioned apples, the second arranged bread in paper bags, and the third prepared labels for meals that needed to be carried to the shelter. Each label listed the meal’s date and the main ingredients. The kitchen did not claim that any meal was free of every possible allergen, so Mara told the volunteers to answer questions by checking the ingredient sheet rather than guessing. She also asked them to keep the serving spoons separate: one for the stew, one for the rice, and one for the carrots. A volunteer noticed that the handle on the rice spoon had a crack. Mara replaced it from the clean utensil drawer before service began.

The updated message from the shelter arrived at 8:20. It said that 18 additional people would need lunch, including several children, and asked whether the kitchen could send the meals by 11:30. Because the extra rice was still dry and the kitchen had enough lentils and broth, Mara approved cooking another pot. If the shelter had asked for more meals than the pantry could support, the team would have called the community center before changing the menu; in this case, there were enough ingredients, and the community center was not contacted. Two volunteers started the extra rice while Priya increased the stew batch. Mara wrote the new total on the whiteboard and told the packing team not to seal the shelter containers until the food had been counted.

At 9:15, a delivery driver arrived with bread that had been ordered for the following week. The invoice showed the later date, so Mara thanked him but did not accept the delivery into the day’s inventory. She called the bakery, and the manager confirmed that the order had been brought a week early by mistake. The driver took the crates back, leaving the kitchen with its original bread supply. That meant the team did not need to change the meal plan or borrow bread from another organization. Ben checked the remaining bags and found two with torn seams; those were kept for the volunteers’ staff meal, while intact bags were set aside for guests.

Service started at 11:45, fifteen minutes later than the shelter’s requested arrival time. The shelter driver had called to say that traffic was moving slowly near the bridge, so the packed containers stayed in the warming cabinet until the van arrived. The volunteers served guests at the kitchen’s front tables while Mara and Leon counted portions for the delivery. They packed 158 complete lunches, then counted the labels again before loading the van. “We have the right number, and the ingredient sheets are on top,” Leon said. Mara checked that the containers were closed and that the hot-food thermometer still showed a safe temperature. The driver signed the handoff sheet at 12:05 and carried the food to the shelter.

After the lunch rush, the team washed cookware, sanitized the counters, and recorded the remaining food. The lentil stew had run out, while some rice and roasted carrots remained. Mara cooled the leftovers according to the kitchen’s storage procedure, labeled the containers with the date and time, and placed them in the refrigerator. The cracked spoon was marked for disposal, and the delivery discrepancy was noted on the inventory form so the next shift would know why the bread count differed from the invoice. Before leaving, the volunteers checked the floor, emptied the compost bin, and returned the clean serving utensils to their drawer. Mara thanked each person by name and left the whiteboard updated for Sunday’s team: 158 lunches served, one early bread delivery returned, and the remaining rice and carrots stored for later use.

The north block of Cedar Lane Orchard uses a low-pressure drip system fed from a lined storage pond. On Monday morning, Mara Chen found a wet strip beside row 18 and a drop in pressure at the far end of the lateral. The pump gauge still showed its usual range, so she checked the filter and the main valve before opening the repair area. The filter screen held a small amount of leaf grit but was not blocked. The valve handle moved freely, and there was no visible leak around its fittings. She recorded the pressure readings and marked the wet ground with two orange flags so the crew could return to the same location after the soil dried.

The affected lateral runs about 110 meters along the lower side of the block. It serves 24 young pear trees and shares a supply manifold with two shorter laterals. The pipe lies under a narrow strip of mulch, with a shallow drainage swale about four meters downhill. The ground was soft from irrigation the previous evening, but there had been no rain for six days. Mara shut the row valve and waited for the line to drain before lifting the mulch. Water continued to seep from one point near a connector, although the rest of the exposed pipe remained dry. That detail suggested a local leak rather than a problem at the manifold.

1. The crew isolated the section between the row valve and the final emitter. Luis Ortega used a hand spade to remove mulch and soil in thin layers, taking care not to pull on the nearby emitter tubing. At a depth of about 12 centimeters, he found a split in the 16-millimeter lateral, roughly 30 centimeters from a barbed coupling. The split was on the underside of the pipe and measured about 18 millimeters. The coupling did not appear cracked, and its barb remained seated. Luis said, “The fitting looks sound; the pipe has opened beside it.” Mara photographed the pipe before cutting it, with a ruler and the row marker visible in the frame.

2. The damaged part was cut out with clean shears. The crew checked the cut ends for flattening and dirt, then trimmed a few millimeters from one end to get a round, clean opening. They used a straight 16-millimeter repair sleeve from the orchard’s parts cabinet and pushed each pipe end fully over the sleeve barbs. The sleeve fit tightly without a clamp. Mara marked the insertion depth with a pencil before joining the pieces, which let her confirm that neither end had shifted while the crew handled the pipe. The repaired length remained aligned with the existing lateral and did not rest against the coupling or a tree stake.

3. Before covering the repair, Mara reopened the row valve slowly. She watched the connection for several minutes while Luis checked the emitter at the end of the line and compared its flow with an emitter on the neighboring row. No water appeared at the cut, and the far-end pressure reading returned close to the measurement from the previous week. The emitter flow looked similar by eye, but the crew did not have a flow meter with them. Mara noted that limitation in the work log rather than recording a measured flow rate. They left the repair exposed during the rest of the test so any new seepage would be easy to see.

4. The soil around the line was still damp, so the crew placed the excavated soil on a tarp instead of piling it against the pipe. They removed two small stones from the trench and checked that the drainage path remained open. The mulch went back only after the repair area stayed dry through a second short test. Luis spread it evenly without pressing it onto the lateral. The orange flags remained in place, and Mara added a small map mark showing the repair’s distance from the row marker. The crew took the tarp and cut pipe back to the equipment shed for disposal and inventory.

The work log includes the date, block, row, pipe size, approximate split length, parts used, and the two pressure readings. Mara attached the before-and-after photographs and noted that the leak was found on the underside of the lateral near the barbed coupling. She also recorded that the screen had leaf grit but was not blocked, since that observation may help if pressure falls again elsewhere in the block. The filter was returned to its housing after inspection, and the main valve remained in its normal operating position. The row valve was left open for scheduled irrigation.

The repair sits in a section where equipment access is limited by the swale and by a line of established pear trees. The tractor cannot pass between the rows when the ground is soft, so the crew brought the spade, shears, sleeve, tarp, and pressure gauge by hand. A shallow rut beside the lower access path had collected water earlier in the season, but it was dry during this visit. Mara asked the crew not to widen the excavation unless the sleeve moved or the leak returned. That kept the disturbed area small and left the nearby feeder roots covered.

During the test, Luis heard a brief hiss from the manifold, then saw that it came from water leaving an air-release point as the line refilled. The sound stopped after the pressure settled. He checked the manifold’s unions and the two neighboring row valves; neither had visible moisture. Mara entered the hiss in her notes because it occurred during the refill, but she did not list it as a leak. If pressure drops again while the filter remains clear, the crew will compare the far-end reading on row 18 with the neighboring rows before opening the repaired section. That condition matters because the shared manifold can affect more than one lateral.

The final inspection covered the pipe alignment, sleeve position, mulch depth, nearby emitters, and the drainage swale. The lateral was not under tension, and the repaired segment had enough room to move slightly with changes in temperature. The two flags and map mark identify the location for a later check without relying on the photographs alone. Mara left the work log in the irrigation shed with the gauge readings and parts count, while the images remained attached to the orchard’s maintenance record. No further excavation was made during this visit, and the surrounding soil was left level with the original grade.

The Thursday delivery for Mara’s stall at North Quay Market was due at 6:15 in the morning, before the public doors opened. She sells vegetables and fruit from the middle row, beside the hall’s north entrance. The order came from Bell & Finch Produce, whose van usually arrives from the depot on Ash Street. Mara had booked the delivery two weeks earlier and sent the final quantities by email on Tuesday. She said the timing mattered because the stall’s first customers often came before seven, and the aisle gets crowded once the bread seller starts unloading.

The order had eight crates of tomatoes, six of pears, four boxes of spinach, three sacks of potatoes, and two trays of herbs. Mara had asked for the tomatoes to be firm rather than fully soft, since she wanted them to last through the weekend. She also requested that the spinach stay in its lidded boxes until she could move it into the cooler. The message did not specify a variety of pear, and Bell & Finch sent Conference pears, as they had done on the previous three orders. Mara said she was slightly concerned that the herbs might be tired after the warm weather, but she had not asked the supplier to replace them or reduce the quantity.

The first van arrived at 6:08, seven minutes before the booked time. Its driver, Joel, parked in the marked loading bay and left the engine running while he spoke with the market caretaker. The bay was free, but a cleaning cart was still near the entrance and made it awkward to turn the trolley. Joel moved the van forward by one marked space, then brought the crates through the north entrance in two trips. He set the tomatoes and pears on the stall’s back table, not on the floor, and put the spinach beside the cooler. The herbs came in a separate shallow tray, with a paper slip showing the order number taped to one corner.

1. Mara checked the delivery against her Tuesday email while Joel read out the item labels. The tomato crates were all there, and the fruit was firm to the touch. One pear box had a damp patch along its lower edge, but there was no split cardboard and no visible fruit underneath it. Mara said, “That corner looks worse than it is, perhaps,” and asked Joel to leave the box on the back table until she had checked the bottom. He waited while she lifted the box with both hands. The base held, and she did not find a bruised pear during that quick check. She did not open the other pear boxes.

2. The spinach count matched the order, though one lid had come loose in transit. Mara closed it again and put all four boxes in the cooler, as she had requested. The sacks of potatoes were stacked beside the stall’s storage cupboard, not in front of it, because the cupboard door swings outward. One sack had a small tear near its stitched top. Mara tied the loose fabric with the spare twine kept in her drawer and said she would check the potatoes when she sorted the display. The tear did not spill any potatoes onto the floor, and Joel noted it on the delivery sheet before asking her to initial the quantity column.

The herbs were not as bright as Mara had hoped, although none of the leaves was visibly broken. She said they were “a little tired, but probably usable,” and left them in their tray rather than putting them on display straight away. Joel wrote down her comment beside the herb line. He did not offer a replacement, and Mara did not ask for one. The tray was set on the back table away from the tomatoes, where the stall’s small fan would not blow packaging onto it. Mara planned to look at the herbs again after she finished arranging the larger items, which usually took her about twenty minutes.

The second van, carrying the bread stall’s shared packing supplies, was expected at 6:30 and had not arrived by the time Joel finished unloading. The caretaker told Mara that if it missed the slot, she could use the side entrance for any later delivery, but she had to call him before moving crates through that route. At 6:34, Mara called the caretaker and said the second van was still not there. He told her to keep the north entrance clear and to use the side entrance if the van came later. Mara repeated that instruction to Joel, although his van had already left the loading bay. She did not move any of her own crates to the side entrance.

After Joel left, Mara placed the tomatoes in two rows on the front table, keeping the firmer crates behind the ones she expected to sell first. She put the pears on the lower shelf so customers would not need to lift them above shoulder height. The damp-corner box stayed on the back table while she worked. She had not decided whether to include those pears in the display, and she said she would make that choice after a closer check. The potatoes remained beside the cupboard until she could sort them, so that the narrow customer aisle stayed clear.

At 6:52, the second van arrived and stopped at the north entrance. Mara spoke with its driver, then called the caretaker again before anything was unloaded. She said the driver had two cartons and a folded stand for the bread stall, and asked whether the side entrance was still the right route. The caretaker’s earlier instruction remained relevant because the north entrance had become busy with other sellers. Mara waited beside the stall while the driver kept the cartons in the van. The spinach remained in the cooler, the herbs remained in their tray on the back table, and the pears in the damp-corner box were still awaiting her closer check.
